claims.text: Increasing chromium content from about 9% to about 12% in ferritic–martensitic steel increases corrosion resistance in supercritical water.
Higher chromium content drives rapid formation of a chromium-enriched oxide film.
The chromium-enriched film is predominantly Cr2O3.
The chromium-enriched oxide film is adherent and acts as a barrier against further oxidation.
Temperature, oxygen concentration, and flow rate are relevant variables affecting oxidation of 9–12 Cr ferritic–martensitic steels in supercritical water.
Supercritical-water conditions are temperatures above 374°C and pressures above 22 MPa.
The specified supercritical-water conditions are representative of both nuclear-power and chemical-processing environments.
Chromium preferentially oxidizes relative to other elements in ferritic–martensitic steel under supercritical-water conditions.
A chromium-rich oxide layer impedes oxygen ingress.
A chromium-rich oxide layer impedes metal dissolution.
Higher-chromium steels exhibit slower oxidation than lower-chromium steels in supercritical water.
Oxidation under the proposed mechanism follows parabolic kinetics.
Higher-chromium steels will have lower weight gain than lower-chromium steels under otherwise identical supercritical-water exposure.
Higher-chromium steels will develop more uniform and adherent chromium-rich oxide layers than lower-chromium steels.
Lower-chromium steels form less protective, non-uniform oxide scales.
The proposed mechanism may extend to similar aqueous environments but may fail in highly acidic or non-aqueous environments.

contradictions.description: The mechanism predicts parabolic oxidation kinetics, whereas the sole cited record explicitly reports a departure of oxidation kinetics from the parabolic law.
